awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  Ultra-Sensitive and Multiplexed Pathogen Profiling for Neonatal Sepsis Detection
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project lies in its potential to transform sepsis diagnostics and patient care, particularly for vulnerable newborns. Globally, sepsis is responsible for up to a third of neonatal deaths, with an increased burden in low- and middle- income countries. Current diagnostic methods rely heavily on blood cultures, which require substantial blood volumes, take 24+ hours to yield results, and frequently produce false negatives. The proposed DNA-based technology seeks to comprehensively identify and quantify pathogens in a few hours from small volumes of blood, critical capabilities for low-birthweight and immunocompromised newborns. The clinical impacts could include more targeted antibiotic therapy and guided therapy durations that could translate to thousands of lives saved annually, shortened hospital stays, and reduced readmission rates. This technology's compatibility with existing digital PCR hardware enables a very capital-efficient development path and reduces barriers to adoption in hospitals given the expanding use of digital PCR in clinical diagnostic laboratories. Enabling routine pathogen testing for sepsis in any community hospital represents a major opportunity. The core proposed technologies can build on a growing installed base of compatible hardware, adding new tests in other diverse applications.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to develop a rapid diagnostic test for sepsis-causing pathogens in plasma samples with available digital PCR hardware that can scale to cover all critical pathogens. Pathogen identification tests must be very sensitive, fast, and able to detect a wide range of organisms. Specific innovations are proposed to make the test suitable for neonates with less than 1 mL of blood per test. Currently, digital PCR-based technologies achieve state-of-the-art sensitivity with results in a few hours but are limited in their panel breadth, typically detecting no more than a dozen analytes simultaneously. DNA sequencing can achieve comprehensive detection but is complex, costly for on-demand use, and much slower than PCR. The proposed technology combines advanced primer design with statistical algorithms to achieve critical features by targeting microbial cell-free DNA in plasma. The research objectives include developing an initial 17-target panel for common sepsis-causing pathogens and achieving analytical sensitivity below 5 genome copies/mL with turnaround time under 4 hours. Anticipated results include demonstration of clinically relevant analytical sensitivity and high analytical specificity in plasma samples.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The Problem

Invasive fungal infections are a major cause of illness and death in immunocompromised patients, including organ transplant recipients, individuals undergoing chemotherapy, and those with blood cancers. These infections are estimated to cause over 2 million deaths worldwide each year, and outcomes are significantly worse when diagnosis is delayed. Despite their severity, these infections remain difficult to diagnose. Current methods are often too slow, lack sensitivity, or can only identify a limited range of fungal species. Because antifungal therapies carry significant toxicity and drug interaction risks, clinicians need rapid and reliable diagnostic confirmation before initiating treatment. This creates a pressing need for a faster, more accurate, and minimally invasive diagnostic approach.

Our Approach

Anvil Diagnostics developed a blood-based diagnostic platform that can simultaneously identify dozens of disease-causing fungi from a standard blood draw. This breadth of coverage is important because many existing tests target only one or a few species, forcing clinicians to order multiple tests or make treatment decisions with incomplete information. MycoScan aims to consolidate this into a single workflow by detecting trace amount of circulating fungal DNA in patient plasma with pan-fungal coverage, avoiding the delays and limitations of culture-based diagnostics and low-resolution biomarker tests. The core innovation is a primer encoding system that assigns each fungal species a unique fluorescent "barcode." Combined with advanced statistical analysis, this allows identification of dozens of species with a single test, which overcomes a key limitation of conventional molecular diagnostics. MycoScan is designed to run on commercially available laboratory instruments, removing the need for hospitals to invest in new equipment.

Key Results

The primary product developed during Phase I was MycoScan, a pan-fungal blood test that distinguishes over 41 clinically relevant fungi. In analytical studies, MycoScan detected fungal DNA at extremely low concentrations, identifying as few as 1 to 5 copies of an organism's DNA per test for most targets. This level of sensitivity is important because fungal DNA circulates in very small quantities in the bloodstream and insufficient sensitivity has hampered the clinical utility of other DNA-based fungal diagnostics. The test demonstrated over 93% analytical specificity when evaluated against healthy donor controls and samples containing bacterial DNA. The complete workflow from collected blood sample to result takes approximately 3.5 hours, meeting the project's target of under four hours.

To demonstrate that the underlying technology extends beyond fungal applications, the team also developed a proof-of-concept bacterial panel that correctly identified 17 bloodstream infection-associated species using the same assay architecture and analytical framework, confirming platform versatility without requiring new innovations.

Early Clinical Evaluation

Exceeding original Phase I objectives, Anvil trialed Beta versions of MycoScan with three independent hospital and university laboratories. Collaborators successfully operated the MycoScan Beta test on their own instruments without on-site training from the Anvil team. MycoScan detected clinically significant fungal pathogens in real patient samples, including specimens that had been stored for extended periods. These pilots provided early validation of manufacturability, shipping stability, usability, and performance outside of Anvil's own laboratory.

Commercial Progress

Customer discovery during Phase I revealed strong clinical demand for improved fungal diagnostics. Clinicians and laboratory directors consistently identified the low diagnostic yield of existing methods and the risks of empiric antifungal therapy as key unmet needs. Based on this feedback, Anvil prioritized the fungal panel for commercialization.

Broader Impacts

Invasive fungal infections contribute to thousands of deaths annually among immunocompromised patients, with many cases going undiagnosed or diagnosed too late for effective intervention. As the number of immunocompromised individuals continues to grow —driven by advances in transplant medicine, expanded use of immunosuppressive therapies, and an aging population — the burden of fungal infections is expected to continue increasing. MycoScan addresses this need by enabling rapid, sensitive, and minimally invasive detection, with the potential to reduce diagnostic delays, guide targeted therapy, and improve patient outcomes. The underlying platform is adaptable to other pathogen classes, supporting future expansion into additional clinical applications. Phase I results demonstrate technical feasibility and position the platform for expanded clinical validation and commercialization.
